passage: I'm Grace, Ankita's roommate. I watched her phone light up all evening with messages from Francis, the friend who skipped her birthday lunch for a beach trip with his office people. His messages were long. "The plan came up last minute, you know how my manager is, I thought you'd be busy anyway, I'll make it up." Ankita read each one and typed back a word or two. "Ok." "Sure." "Got it." I asked if she was still angry. She shrugged. "I don't need the timetable of his weekend. I just want him to get that I sat in that café alone for forty minutes." Then she put the phone face down and went back to her book, though I didn't see her turn a page.

"About Saturday," he began. "The traffic was mad, and then my cousin called, and—"

I still have the chat from that week. I'm Ayesha, and I'd waited three months for my first solo exhibition at the college gallery. Inder had promised to come. He didn't.

The next morning he messaged a long paragraph: the bus, a headache, his project partner. It went on and on. At the end: "So we're good, right? 😊"

I typed "ok."

He sent another message. "Are you mad?" I typed "no."

The truth was I didn't need reasons. I didn't care about the bus. I wanted him to say: you knew how much it mattered to me, and you weren't there. I wanted to see if he understood what it cost me to look at the door all evening.

Until he did, short answers were all I had. I wasn't punishing him. I was waiting.

qa.q: How long had Ayesha waited for the exhibition?
qa.a: Ayesha had waited three months.

qa.q: What was Ayesha hoping for behind the short replies?
qa.a: Ayesha felt let down and hurt, and was waiting for Inder to acknowledge what missing the exhibition had cost, not for more excuses.

qa.q: What could Inder do now to reach Ayesha?
qa.a: He could drop the reasons and say plainly that he wasn't there on a day that mattered, and that he's sorry.

qa.a: Inder may read them as coldness or anger and want the tension gone quickly, not realising Ayesha needs acknowledgment.
